Dusky antechinus neonates emerge at a remarkably diminutive size, with a newborn wet weight of just 0.0164 grams [Wwb = 0.0164 grams]. This extreme altricial state, typical of many dasyurid marsupials, reflects a short gestation period of 28 days [tg = 28 days] measured at a maternal body temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. Following birth, the tiny pups, each weighing less than a grain of rice, must immediately crawl to the mother's pouch and attach to a teat for continuous suckling. Their growth during this early nursing phase is rapid but they remain entirely dependent on milk for several weeks. The reproductive strategy of this species is characterized by a single, synchronized annual breeding event. Females produce a single litter of eight pups per year [Ri = eight pups per year], resulting in a yearly reproductive rate of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This synchronized reproductive effort is a well-known life-history hallmark of the genus Antechinus, with all males dying shortly after the mating period due to stress-induced physiological collapse. The complete dependency of the young on the mother during lactation places immense energetic demands on the female.

By the time they are ready to transition to solid food, the weaning mass of the offspring has increased considerably to 15 grams [Wwx = 15 grams], achieved approximately 94 days after birth [tx = approximately 94 days after birth] at a body temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. This period marks the end of the suckling juvenile phase and the onset of nutritional independence for the young. Weaning represents a critical juncture in the life cycle of the dusky antechinus, as juveniles must now forage on their own for insects and other small invertebrates in the dense leaf litter of the forest floor. The energetic efficiency of this foraging, coupled with the metabolic costs of growth and thermoregulation, dictates the survival rates during the sub-adult stage. The duration from birth to weaning, at 94 days [tx = 94 days], is relatively brief compared to many other small mammals, reflecting the intense selective pressure of a semelparous life history where the entire annual cohort must mature and reproduce within a single calendar year at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. The weaned juveniles then enter a period of intensive mass accumulation and physiological development to prepare for their own reproductive future.

Puberty in the dusky antechinus is reached at 330 days after birth [tp = 330 days after birth] at a body temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], a developmental milestone that coincides with the approach of the highly synchronized winter breeding season. This timing of gonadal maturation ensures that both males and females are reproductively competent when the brief mating window arrives, maximizing the probability of successful fertilization for the entire population. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, individuals continue to invest in somatic growth, with the ultimate wet weight of an adult averaging 67 grams [Wwi = 67 grams]. This adult body mass is intermediate among antechinus species, reflecting a trade-off between the energetic demands of endothermy in cool, wet forests and the need to accumulate sufficient reserves for the exhaustive breeding season. The males, driven by extreme testosterone surges, experience a catastrophic deterioration of their physiology after mating, leading to universal male die-off. Females, however, survive to rear the litter and, in rare cases, may live to breed in a second season, though most females also die after weaning their first and only litter.

The lifespan of the dusky antechinus is inherently constrained by its semelparous reproductive strategy, with a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 1204 days [am = approximately 1204 days] under average thermal conditions of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. Given that most individuals only survive a single breeding season, this figure primarily describes the rare individuals who manage to survive into a second year. The physiological cost of reproduction is immense: during the breeding period, males exhibit elevated levels of free cortisol that suppress the immune system and cause gastric ulceration, leading to their death shortly after mating. This post-reproductive mortality is absolute in males and nearly so in females, who often succumb to the energetic drain of lactation just as their young become independent. Basal metabolic rate has been measured in this species at 36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This moderately high metabolic rate, typical of small insectivorous marsupials, reflects the energetic cost of maintaining endothermy and supporting the high activity levels required for foraging in Tasmania's cool, wet environments.

Field studies of the dusky antechinus have consistently documented the tight coupling between metabolic expenditure and life-history scheduling. The resting metabolic rate of 36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at the thermoneutral temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C] provides a baseline for understanding the immense energetic burden of lactation. The females, who must sustain a litter of eight pups that each weigh 15 grams [Wwx = 15 grams] at weaning, face a significant metabolic challenge. During peak lactation, their food intake can increase by over 50 percent above normal to meet the demands of milk production. The wet weight at birth of just 0.0164 grams [Wwb = 0.0164 grams] underscores the necessity of this prolonged and costly parental investment. Litter size is invariant across most populations, with females producing eight offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = eight offspring per reproductive event] regardless of local resource conditions, a strategy that differs markedly from the more flexible litter sizes observed in some other dasyurids. Comparative studies within the genus Antechinus suggest that the dusky antechinus, with its relatively large adult size of 67 grams [Wwi = 67 grams], occupies a distinct niche in the cool, mesic forests of southeastern Australia.
